title: Hurricane Quillon — FDEM cash advance allocation
input:
Hurricane Quillon made landfall near Panama City Beach, FL on 2026-10-10 as a Category 2 hurricane. Ten Panhandle counties are under a state of emergency. FDEM has $46,750,000 in direct operational cash for rapid Category A/B emergency work and must decide how much to advance to each county before any federal major disaster declaration is approved. Supporting documents 01-09 are attached.

# Executive Order EX-1 (Emergency Management - Hurricane Quillon Landfall)

STATE OF FLORIDA — OFFICE OF THE GOVERNOR

WHEREAS, on October 10, 2026, Hurricane Quillon made landfall near Panama City Beach, Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour; and

WHEREAS, Hurricane Quillon generated storm surge exceeding 8 feet in Apalachee Bay, severing electricity to over 385,000 customers across ten Panhandle counties;

NOW, THEREFORE, the Governor, by virtue of Article IV, Section 1(a) of the Florida Constitution and Chapter 252, Florida Statutes, declares a STATE OF EMERGENCY in Bay, Gulf, Franklin, Wakulla, Escambia, Santa Rosa, Okaloosa, Walton, Washington, and Calhoun Counties.

SECTION 1. DESIGNATION OF STATE COORDINATING OFFICER
The Director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM) is designated as the State Coordinating Officer (SCO) to execute the State Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan (CEMP).

SECTION 2. FINANCIAL AND RESERVE AUTHORIZATION
Pursuant to Section 252.371, Florida Statutes, the transfer of $150,000,000.00 from unallocated General Revenue reserves into the Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund is authorized.

Issued at Tallahassee, October 10, 2026. (Signed) Governor

# Memorandum: Authorization of Emergency Reserve Transfer

TO: Board of Commissioners & Legislative Budget Commission
FROM: Director of Budget and Financial Operations, FDEM
DATE: October 10, 2026
SUBJECT: Authorization of Emergency Reserve Transfer - Hurricane Quillon Response

## I. Purpose & authority
Pursuant to Executive Order EX-1 and Section 252.371, Florida Statutes, this memorandum establishes the fiscal accounting protocol for transferring $150,000,000.00 into the Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund (Account: FDEM-EPRF-2026-QUILLON).

## II. Funding allocation breakdown
| Line | Amount (USD) |
| --- | ---: |
| 1. State Non-Federal PA Match Obligation (17.5% of $590M Total Direct Cost) | 103,250,000.00 |
| 2. FDEM Direct Operational Cash Liquidity (Rapid Category A/B Emergency Work) | 46,750,000.00 |
| **Total authorized emergency transfer** | **150,000,000.00** |

## III. Reconciliation balance
| Share | Amount (USD) |
| --- | ---: |
| Federal PA Share (75%) | 442,500,000.00 |
| State PA Match (17.5%) | 103,250,000.00 |
| Local Sub-Recipient Share (7.5%) | 44,250,000.00 |
| **Total direct damage baseline** | **590,000,000.00** (Variance: $0.00) |

SHA256: 455475085194ccc0598ec4109d359d6a6c8fec03513dd277e8b69badc7d3e442

# Declaration and operations status (Hurricane Quillon), as of 2026-10-11 18:00 ET

## Declarations
- State of emergency: declared 2026-10-10 under Executive Order EX-1 (10 counties).
- Federal emergency declaration (Category B): requested 2026-10-10; status pending.
- Federal major disaster declaration (Public Assistance Categories A-G): request in preparation; not yet submitted; joint preliminary damage assessments scheduled to begin 2026-10-13.
- Until a major disaster declaration is approved, no federal Public Assistance funds are obligated. The 75% federal share in 03 and 04 is an assumption.

## Operations
- State Operations Center: Level 1 activation.
- Urban Search & Rescue: Teams 1 and 3 deployed (Bay, Gulf, Franklin). 214 rescues reported; search complete in Bay, ongoing in Gulf and Franklin.
- Mutual aid: EMAC requests for 2 incident management teams and 40 line crews submitted; 1 team accepted.
- Utility restoration estimates: Escambia, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa 85% restored by 2026-10-17; Bay, Walton, Washington, Calhoun 85% by 2026-10-21; Gulf, Franklin, Wakulla coastal areas no estimate (transmission lines down, roads cut).
- Boil-water notices: Gulf, Franklin, Wakulla, Calhoun (all systems).

## Open unknowns (not available to the planner as of this report)
- Final damage totals; the $590,000,000 baseline is a state preliminary estimate.
- Insurance recoveries for public buildings (Category E).
- Whether the federal cost share will be raised above 75%.
- Debris volume in Franklin and Wakulla coastal areas (no access).

# Declaration and operations status (Hurricane Quillon), as of 2026-10-11 18:00 ET

## Declarations
- State of emergency: declared 2026-10-10 under Executive Order EX-1 (10 counties).
- Federal emergency declaration (Category B): requested 2026-10-10; status pending.
- Federal major disaster declaration (Public Assistance Categories A-G): request in preparation; not yet submitted; joint preliminary damage assessments scheduled to begin 2026-10-13.
- Until a major disaster declaration is approved, no federal Public Assistance funds are obligated. The 75% federal share in 03 and 04 is an assumption.

## Operations
- State Operations Center: Level 1 activation.
- Urban Search & Rescue: Teams 1 and 3 deployed (Bay, Gulf, Franklin). 214 rescues reported; search complete in Bay, ongoing in Gulf and Franklin.
- Mutual aid: EMAC requests for 2 incident management teams and 40 line crews submitted; 1 team accepted.
- Utility restoration estimates: Escambia, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa 85% restored by 2026-10-17; Bay, Walton, Washington, Calhoun 85% by 2026-10-21; Gulf, Franklin, Wakulla coastal areas no estimate (transmission lines down, roads cut).
- Boil-water notices: Gulf, Franklin, Wakulla, Calhoun (all systems).

## Open unknowns (not available to the planner as of this report)
- Final damage totals; the $590,000,000 baseline is a state preliminary estimate.
- Insurance recoveries for public buildings (Category E).
- Whether the federal cost share will be raised above 75%.
- Debris volume in Franklin and Wakulla coastal areas (no access).

objective: Allocate the $46,750,000 FDEM direct operational cash pool across the 10 declared counties for Category A/B emergency work, keeping at least $4,675,000 in state reserve, prioritizing life safety and counties that cannot front costs.
stakeholder_needs: Bay: landfall county, largest damage, can front costs ~60 days. Escambia, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Walton: large reserves, limited advance need. Gulf, Franklin, Calhoun: cannot meet local share; Franklin payroll at risk; Calhoun requests full advance. Wakulla, Washington: under 3 weeks of cash; Wakulla needs advance to start debris removal. Hospitals on generator in Bay, Escambia, Gulf, Franklin, Calhoun need fuel priority, funded within each county's own allocation.

sources.content:
# Executive Order EX-1 (Emergency Management - Hurricane Quillon Landfall)

STATE OF FLORIDA — OFFICE OF THE GOVERNOR

WHEREAS, on October 10, 2026, Hurricane Quillon made landfall near Panama City Beach, Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour; and

WHEREAS, Hurricane Quillon generated storm surge exceeding 8 feet in Apalachee Bay, severing electricity to over 385,000 customers across ten Panhandle counties;

NOW, THEREFORE, the Governor, by virtue of Article IV, Section 1(a) of the Florida Constitution and Chapter 252, Florida Statutes, declares a STATE OF EMERGENCY in Bay, Gulf, Franklin, Wakulla, Escambia, Santa Rosa, Okaloosa, Walton, Washington, and Calhoun Counties.

SECTION 1. DESIGNATION OF STATE COORDINATING OFFICER
The Director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM) is designated as the State Coordinating Officer (SCO) to execute the State Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan (CEMP).

SECTION 2. FINANCIAL AND RESERVE AUTHORIZATION
Pursuant to Section 252.371, Florida Statutes, the transfer of $150,000,000.00 from unallocated General Revenue reserves into the Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund is authorized.

Issued at Tallahassee, October 10, 2026. (Signed) Governor

Release Date:

April 24, 2026

LAKE MARY, Fla. — FEMA announced nearly $97 million in funding to support recovery for past disasters in Florida for Public Assistance projects. Through Public Assistance, FEMA empowers state and local communities to recover following a major disaster, including debris removal, emergency protective measures and the repair or replacement of public infrastructure damaged by recent disasters. [...] More than $19 million to reimburse costs for power restoration and distribution systems, including $11.2 million for Lee County Electric Cooperative for Hurricane Ian, $4 million for Sumter Electric Cooperative following Hurricane Milton and $1.1 million for Central Florida Electric Cooperative for Hurricane Helene.
 More than $17.3 million for countywide debris removal following Hurricane Ian in Sarasota County.
 Nearly $12.3 million for the City of Tallahassee’s debris removal and emergency response following severe storms in 2024. [...] FEMA is reimbursing these costs at no less than 75% federal share. Since January 2025, more than $2 billion has been provided to Florida to support the state’s infrastructure repair and rebuilding. We will continue to work closely with Florida to support communities through the state-led recovery efforts.

sources.content:
Course Overview, Course Goal, and Objectives

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| |  | | --- | | Welcome to the Emergency Protective Measures course.  The course will provide an overview of Emergency Protective Measures under the FEMA Public Assistance Program. By the end of the course, State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial Applicants and Recipients will be able to accurately capture Emergency Protective Measures activities and document costs concerning actual overtime based on payroll policies, equipment usage, and reasonable materials purchases.  Upon completion of this course, participants will be able to:   * Define Emergency Protective Measures * Identify Emergency Protective Measures eligible for FEMA Public Assistance Program grant funding * Describe documentation requirements that support application for reimbursement of Emergency Protective Measures  Select this link to access the Public Assistance acronym list. != 'undefined' ) {NewGrouping('966520524153250F9AFA130B003A6D69','1');}) | |

Lesson 1 Overview and Objectives

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| |  | | --- | | This lesson provides a brief overview of Emergency Protective Measures.  Upon completion of this lesson, participants will be able to:   * Identify administrative requirements of the course * State the goals and objectives of the course * Define Emergency Protective Measures | |

Public Assistance Categories of Work

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | | |  | | --- | | Within the Public Assistance Program, there are two general types of work: Emergency Work and Permanent Work. To facilitate the processing of Public Assistance grant funding, FEMA separates Emergency Work into two categories, based on the type of work performed. Permanent Work is separated into five categories based on facility types. | | Select this link for a full image description. != 'undefined' ) {NewGrouping('86772052415324B1DAED130B003791E2','1');}) | | |

Emergency Work

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  | | --- | --- | | |  | | --- | | Public Assistance Emergency Work is work which must be done immediately to:   * Save lives * Protect public health and safety * Protect improved property * Eliminate or lessen an immediate threat of additional damage   Emergency Work is made up of two Categories of Work:   * Category A - Debris Removal * Category B - Emergency Protective Measures   An Applicant has six months from the declaration or designation date to complete their eligible Emergency Work, unless the Recipient or FEMA authorizes an extension. | | |

Emergency Protective Measures

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  | | --- | --- | | |  | | --- | | This course focuses on Category B, Emergency Protective Measures, of Emergency Work under the Public Assistance program.  Emergency Protective Measures are temporary measures taken against an incident. As outlined in the Public Assistance Program and Policy Guide, 2.VI.B,  Emergency Protective Measures are actions taken before, during, and after an incident to save lives, protect public health and safety, and prevent damage to improved public and private property. | | |

Emergency Protective Measures Eligibility

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  | | --- | --- | | |  | | --- | | Emergency Protective Measures conducted before, during, and after an incident are generally eligible if the measures:   * Eliminate or lessen immediate threats to lives, public health, or safety * Eliminate or lessen immediate threats of significant additional damage to improved public or private property in a cost-effective manner   Emergency Protective Measures eligibility is typically based on evaluation of the immediate threat and legal authority to perform the work.  FEMA may require validation by State, Local, Tribal, or Territorial government officials that a threat exists, including:   * Identification and evaluation of the threat * Recommendations of the work necessary to minimize the threat | | |

Emergency Protective Measures Cost-effectiveness

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| |  | | --- | | Another aspect of eligibility is cost-effectiveness. Certain projects must be cost-effective for Applicants to be eligible for grant funding from the Public Assistance program.   * Emergency Protective Measures that eliminate or lessen an immediate threat to lives, public health, and/or safety **do not** have to be cost-effective * Emergency Protective Measures that eliminate or lessen an immediate threat to protect improved property **must be** cost-effective | |

Linking Emergency Protective Measures to a Declared Event

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| |  | | --- | | As stated previously, Emergency Protective Measures conducted before, during, and after an incident are generally eligible.  Some activities that may qualify as Emergency Protective Measures include:   * Firefighting * Search and rescue * Evacuation and sheltering   Throughout response operations, it is important to track activities that are potentially eligible for reimbursement under the Public Assistance grant program. Without tracking Emergency Protective Measures, an Applicant may jeopardize Public Assistance grant funding. | |

Lesson 1 Summary

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| |  | | --- | | Emergency Protective Measures are temporary measures taken against an incident.  In this lesson, participants learned how to:   * Identify administrative requirements of the course * State the goals and objectives of the course * Define emergency protective measures   The next lesson provides an in-depth look at the activities that qualify as Emergency Protective Measures eligible under the Public Assistance Program. | |

Hurricane Milton Recovery: Brief Overview of FEMA Programs and Resources 

Updated October 13, 2024 (IN12438) 

Introduction

On October 9, 2024, Hurricane Milton made landfall as a Category 4 hurricane in Florida's Tampa Bay area bringing heavy rain, storm surge, and floods to many counties on the coast and in the interior of the state. Some areas in the state are still actively recovering from Hurricane Helene.

President Biden had previously issued an emergency declaration for this storm on October 7, under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act(the Stafford Act, P.L. 93-288, as amended; 42 U.S.C. §§5121 et seq.), authorizing Public Assistance (PA) for emergency protective measuresput into action beginning October 5, 2024. On October 8,2024, President Biden issued another emergency declaration authorizing federal assistance to Seminole Tribe of Florida.

As of October 11, President Biden declared a major disaster for Hurricane Milton in Florida, authorizing PA, Individual Assistance, and Hazard Mitigation Assistance. President Biden also increased the federal share of eligible response costs; the federal government will cover 100% of eligible costs of PA provided for emergency protective measures and debris removal for a period of 90 days.

The situation remains dynamic; additional declarations, or additional forms of assistance are expected given Milton's impact.

Information about state and county disaster assistance is published in FEMA's declaration database. FEMA's Hurricane Milton web p a ge provides information on how to apply for disaster assistance. FEMA has also created another site to dispel rumors and misinformation related to aid to survivors, evacuation, and relief funding.

FEMA Emergency and Major Disaster Assistance

FEMA provides three major categories of disaster assistance, some of which may be available pursuant to an emergency declaration and/or a major disaster declaration:

*   _Public Assistance_(PA) provides grants and direct assistance to state, tribal, territorial, and local governments, and certain private nonprofit organizations, for emergency work (e.g., debris removal and emergency protective measures), and permanent work (for rebuilding and replacement of disaster-damaged facilities). 
*   _Individual Assistance_(IA) supports disaster survivors, including through grants of financial assistance and direct assistance to affected individuals and households for housing and financial assistance for other needs, and crisis counseling (both may be authorized pursuant to either an emergency or major disaster declaration), as well as case management services, legal services, and disaster unemployment assistance (may only be authorized pursuant to a major disaster declaration). 
*   _Hazard Mitigation Grant Program_(HMGP) funds mitigation and resiliency projects and programs, typically across the entire state or territory (can only be authorized pursuant to a major disaster declaration). 

The forms of assistance authorized by a declaration may vary by the designated areas, per the declaration (subject to amendment). The President can also amend emergency and major disaster declarations to decrease the cost-share requirements for PA.

National Flood Insurance Program

The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) is the primary source of flood insurance coverage for residential properties. Homeowners and tenants with NFIP flood insurance can make flood damage claims using the normal NFIP claims process. There does not have to be an emergency or disaster declaration in order to make an NFIP claim. Policyholders can make a claim as soon as they can safely return to their property to document the damage.

As of September 30, 2024, the NFIP had $5.001 billion available to pay claims. If claims from Hurricane Milton are more than this, FEMA could borrow up to $9.9 billion from the Treasury. FEMA could also potentially receive up to $619.5 million of reinsuranceif losses from Hurricane Milton are between $7 billion and $11 billion. The NFIP is currently authorized until December 20, 2024.

Federal Funding for Disaster Response and Recovery

While it is not the only source of federal funding for disaster assistance, FEMA's Disaster Relief Fund (DRF) is the primary funding source for federal government response and recovery activities. As a result, its level of unobligated funds is often used as a proxy for the overall availability of federal resources for response and recovery.

On August 7, 2024,prior to the development of Hurricane Helene, FEMA announced the implementation of immediate needs funding (INF) restrictions, as a result of the unobligated balance in the DRF for major disasters being at risk of depletion before the end of FY2024. INF slows obligations for long-term recovery and mitigation projects in favor of preserving resources for response and recovery activities. Although annual appropriations have not been enacted for FEMA as of the date on this Insight, on September 26, 2024, President Biden signed into law a continuing resolution(P.L. 118-83) that provides $20.26 billion in temporary budget authority for the DRF, which became available October 1. When those funds became available, FEMA lifted INF restrictions and resumed obligating funds for more than $8 billion of long-term recovery and mitigation projects that had been delayed.

These funds will be available for Stafford Act disaster assistance programs until December 20, 2024, or until FEMA's annual appropriations are enacted, whichever comes first. If the CR expires, that temporary budget authority will no longer be available, and FEMA's disaster response and recovery functions will be severely constrained.

sources.content:
About

# How many disasters are declared in Florida?

Refreshed monthly

On average, five disasters are declared per year. This figure is based on the most recent 5 full years of Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) data.

As of September 3, two disasters have been declared in Florida in 2026. In 2025, there were zero declarations.

A disaster declaration is more than just recognizing an event—it's a formal request for federal aid when state, local, or tribal resources are overwhelmed. The president approves these declarations when they determine that federal support is necessary.

Declarations vary due to the type and severity of disasters, whether the president approves requests for federal assistance, and other factors.

2

disasters have been declared in Florida from January through September 3, 2026

0

disasters have been declared in Florida in 2025

5

disasters have been declared yearly on average (2021–2025)

The primary two disaster declarations are major disaster and emergency.

* A **major disaster** declaration applies to hurricanes, tornadoes, snowstorms, floods, earthquakes, wildfires, volcanic eruptions, landslides, mudslides, droughts, explosions, and other severe natural events. These typically cause widespread damage requiring long-term recovery efforts.
* An **emergency declaration** is issued when the president determines federal assistance is needed to protect lives, property, or public health and safety. Aid is capped at $5 million and is for urgent crises. These can include public health emergencies (such as COVID-19), terrorist attacks, power outages, or events related to natural disasters.

A third type of declaration, fire management, applies to managing and suppressing either a single large blaze or multiple smaller fires. While fires can also be part of major disasters or emergencies, fire management is a separate category because the declaration process differs: instead of the longer timelines for other declarations, these expedited decisions are usually made within a few hours.

The president must approve all declarations. The federal aid available depends on what kind of disaster is declared. In most cases, governors request these declarations, though tribal nations may also submit requests independently.

## Florida declared 25 disasters in the last 5 years.

Number of disaster declarations by disaster incident type, January 1980–September 3, 2026

## What is the most common disaster in Florida?

In the last 5 years, hurricanes have been 11 out of the state's 25 disasters, making them the most common declaration in that time frame.

In 2020, COVID-19 accounted for four biological emergency declarations that year. States can have multiple declarations for a single disaster event: both by the state and native American tribes, and for major disaster and emergency declarations.

Since 1980, fires have accounted for 69 (40.8%) of all disaster declarations in Florida, the highest of any disaster type. In that same time frame, there have been 169 total declarations across 11 disaster categories.

sources.content:
FEMA Logo

Apply for Assistance

# Generator

Generators are emergency equipment that provide a secondary source of power. Generators and related equipment (e.g., hook-ups) are eligible under the HMGP and PDM provided that they are cost-effective, contribute to a long-term solution to the problem they are intended to address, and meet other program eligibility criteria, which include the following: [...] HMGP: A permanently installed generator that is a stand-alone project can be considered under regular HMGP funding if the generator protects a critical facility. Critical facilities may include police and fire stations, hospitals, and water and sewer treatment facilities. A generator that is a component of a larger project (e.g., elevation of a lift station) can also be funded under regular HMGP funding and the use of aggregation is permitted. Portable generators are eligible provided that they meet all HMGP requirements as described in 44 C.F.R. § 206.434. Stand-alone generator projects that cannot be determined cost-effective via standard HMA benefit-cost methodology may be eligible under the 5 Percent Initiative. See Part IX, A.10 for additional information about the 5 Percent [...] PDM Program: Generators and/or related equipment purchases (e.g., generator hook-ups) are eligible when the generator directly relates to the hazards being mitigated and is part of a larger project.'

###### Department of Homeland Security

###### Federal Emergency Management Agency

# AGENCY:

Federal Emergency Management Agency, DHS.

# ACTION:

Notice.

# SUMMARY:

This is a notice of the Presidential declaration of a major disaster for the State of Florida (FEMA-4834-DR), dated October 11, 2024, and related determinations.

# DATES:

The declaration was issued October 11, 2024.

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Dean Webster, Office of Response and Recovery, Federal Emergency Management Agency, 500 C Street SW, Washington, DC 20472, (202) 646-2833.

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

Notice is hereby given that, in a letter dated October 11, 2024, the President issued a major disaster declaration under the authority of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, 42 U.S.C. 5121
*et seq.*
(the “Stafford Act”), as follows:

I have determined that the damage in certain areas of the State of Florida resulting from Hurricane Milton beginning on October 5, 2024, and continuing, is of sufficient severity and magnitude to warrant a major disaster declaration under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, 42 U.S.C. 5121
*et seq.*
(the “Stafford Act”). Therefore, I declare that such a major disaster exists in the State of Florida.

In order to provide Federal assistance, you are hereby authorized to allocate from funds available for these purposes such amounts as you find necessary for Federal disaster assistance and administrative expenses.

You are authorized to provide Individual Assistance and assistance for debris removal and emergency protective measures (Categories A and B), including direct Federal assistance, under the Public Assistance program in the designated areas, Hazard Mitigation throughout the State, and any other forms of assistance under the Stafford Act that you deem appropriate subject to completion of Preliminary Damage Assessments.

Consistent with the requirement that Federal assistance is supplemental, any Federal funds provided under the Stafford Act for Hazard Mitigation and Other Needs Assistance under section 408 will be limited to 75 percent of the total eligible costs. Federal funds provided under the Stafford Act for Public Assistance also will be limited to 75 percent of the total eligible costs, with the exception of projects that meet the eligibility criteria for a higher Federal cost-sharing percentage in FEMA's Public Assistance Mitigation Cost Share Incentives Policy. For a 90-day period of the State's choosing within the first 120 days from the start of the incident period, you are authorized to fund assistance for debris removal and emergency protective measures, including direct Federal assistance, at 100 percent of the total eligible costs.

Further, you are authorized to make changes to this declaration for the approved assistance to the extent allowable under the Stafford Act.

The time period prescribed for the implementation of section 310(a), Priority to Certain Applications for Public Facility and Public Housing Assistance, 42 U.S.C. 5153, shall be for a period not to exceed six months after the date of this declaration.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) hereby gives notice that pursuant to the authority vested in the Administrator, under Executive Order 12148, as amended, John E. Brogan, of FEMA is appointed to act as the Federal Coordinating Officer for this major disaster.

The following areas of the State of Florida have been designated as adversely affected by this major disaster:

Brevard, Charlotte, Citrus, Clay, Collier, DeSoto, Duval, Flagler, Glades, Hardee, Hendry, Hernando, Highlands, Hillsborough, Indian River, Lake, Lee, Manatee, Marion, Martin, Okeechobee, Orange, Osceola, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas, Polk, Putnam, Sarasota, Seminole, St. Johns, St. Lucie, Sumter, and Volusia Counties and the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida for Individual Assistance.
( printed page 97019)

Brevard, Charlotte, Citrus, Clay, Collier, DeSoto, Duval, Flagler, Glades, Hardee, Hendry, Hernando, Highlands, Hillsborough, Indian River, Lake, Lee, Manatee, Marion, Martin, Okeechobee, Orange, Osceola, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas, Polk, Putnam, Sarasota, Seminole, St. Johns, St. Lucie, Sumter, and Volusia Counties and the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida for debris removal and emergency protective measures (Categories A and B), including direct federal assistance, under the Public Assistance program.

All areas within the State of Florida are eligible for assistance under the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program.

The following Catalog of Federal Domestic Assistance Numbers (CFDA) are to be used for reporting and drawing funds: 97.030, Community Disaster Loans; 97.031, Cora Brown Fund; 97.032, Crisis Counseling; 97.033, Disaster Legal Services; 97.034, Disaster Unemployment Assistance (DUA); 97.046, Fire Management Assistance Grant; 97.048, Disaster Housing Assistance to Individuals and Households In Presidentially Declared Disaster Areas; 97.049, Presidentially Declared Disaster Assistance—Disaster Housing Operations for Individuals and Households; 97.050, Presidentially Declared Disaster Assistance to Individuals and Households—Other Needs; 97.036, Disaster Grants—Public Assistance (Presidentially Declared Disasters); 97.039, Hazard Mitigation Grant.

rounds.effect: Extracting FEMA PAPPG v5 Category B Emergency Protective Measures eligibility criteria for generator fuel and payroll reimbursement requirements to address objections O1, O2, O5, O6, O9, O10, O11.

assessments.negotiator: Extracting FEMA PAPPG v5 Category B Emergency Protective Measures eligibility criteria for generator fuel and payroll reimbursement requirements to address objections O1, O2, O5, O6, O9, O10, O11.
assessments.analyst: Challenging the Negotiator's proposal on three material grounds: (1) Hospital generator fuel costs are embedded in county allocations but fuel contract pricing and FEMA reimbursement eligibility for generator fuel under Category B emergency protective measures are unconfirmed (D8 shows fuel contract pricing not confirmed; S12/S13 describe Category B eligible work but don't confirm generator fuel eligibility). (2) Franklin County's $320K payroll gap is included in its $1.87M allocation as 'payroll bridge' but FEMA PA reimbursement for payroll requires specific pre-disaster documentation policies (S15 shows FEMA scrutinizes payroll documentation policies; eligibility not confirmed for Franklin's payroll bridge). (3) The 12.2% proportional reduction for five fiscally stronger counties uses D5 allocation ratios as baseline, but D5 and D9 state final damage assessments are preliminary and may alter allocation ratios; the 12.2% reduction lacks a documented methodology tied to fiscal capacity metrics. Also requesting evidence on federal declaration timeline and fuel contract pricing.
assessments.risk: Challenging the Negotiator's proposal on three critical risk grounds: (1) The 10% state reserve ($4.675M) is untested against the multi-month federal reimbursement timeline; D9 confirms no federal major disaster declaration submitted yet and D7/D9 indicate reimbursement typically months after obligation, while five counties have <3 weeks cash on hand (Franklin 7 days, Gulf 9, Calhoun 5, Wakulla 18, Washington 12). The reserve may be exhausted before any federal reimbursement arrives. (2) Franklin County's $320K payroll bridge embedded in its $1.87M allocation assumes FEMA PA payroll reimbursement eligibility, but FEMA PA requires pre-disaster documentation policies that withstand scrutiny (S15: 'FEMA only reimburses labor costs consistent with Applicant's written policy in place and used prior to the incident'); Franklin's payroll policies not verified as FEMA-compliant (S15), creating reimbursement risk for the advance. (3) Hospital generator fuel costs embedded in five county allocations (Bay, Escambia, Gulf, Franklin, Calhoun) but FEMA Category B eligibility for generator fuel costs not confirmed; D8 shows 310,000 gallons fuel under contract but pricing unknown, and FEMA PA policy guides (S11, S26) do not confirm generator fuel reimbursement eligibility under Category B emergency protective measures. Also flagging the Analyst's O3: the 12.2% proportional reduction uses preliminary D5 allocation ratios that D9 states are preliminary and may change after joint damage assessments beginning 2026-10-13.
assessments.strategy: Challenging the Negotiator's proposal on four strategic grounds: (1) Single-phase allocation commits $42.075M (90% of cash pool) before federal declaration timeline is known; D9 confirms no major disaster declaration submitted, joint assessments begin 2026-10-13, reimbursement typically months after obligation. A phased allocation preserving additional reserve would better manage multi-month reimbursement risk. (2) The 12.2% uniform reduction across five fiscally stronger counties ignores their varying cash-on-hand (Bay 45 days, Escambia 60, Okaloosa 55, Santa Rosa 40, Walton 50 per D7); reduction should be tiered by fiscal capacity to optimize cash deployment. (3) Hospital generator fuel costs embedded in five county allocations but FEMA Category B eligibility for generator fuel not confirmed; S11, S15, S26 describe Category B eligible work but do not confirm generator fuel reimbursement eligibility. (4) Franklin County's $320K payroll bridge assumes FEMA-compliant pre-disaster payroll policies; S15 confirms FEMA scrutinizes written policies in place pre-disaster and post-disaster changes are not accepted, creating advance reimbursement risk. Also requesting evidence on federal declaration timeline and fuel contract pricing.
assessments.stability: As Stability, I assess the Negotiator's proposal for longer-term fiscal sustainability, implementation dependencies on federal declaration and reimbursement rules, and equitable distribution of benefits and burdens across counties with vastly different fiscal capacities. Three material objections arise: (1) Generator fuel eligibility under Category B is unconfirmed in current FEMA PAPPG v5; the proposal embeds fuel costs in five county allocations but S30 indicates FEMA takes a narrow view of eligible Emergency Protective Measures, creating reimbursement risk for allocated funds. (2) Franklin County's $320K payroll bridge assumes FEMA PA payroll reimbursement eligibility, but S15 confirms FEMA only reimburses labor costs consistent with pre-disaster written policies; Franklin's payroll documentation policies are unverified, creating advance reimbursement risk. (3) The 12.2% uniform reduction across five fiscally stronger counties lacks a documented, defensible methodology tied to quantified fiscal capacity metrics (days of cash on hand: 45, 60, 55, 40, 50; reserve adequacy ratios vary widely), creating arbitrary and potentially inequitable burden distribution. The single-phase commitment of 90% of the cash pool before the federal declaration timeline is known (D9: joint assessments begin 2026-10-13) creates implementation dependency risk if reimbursement rules exclude embedded costs.

findings.explanation: Propose allocating $42,075,000 of the $46,750,000 FDEM direct operational cash pool across 10 counties for Category A/B emergency work, maintaining the required $4,675,000 (10%) state reserve. scenario.narrative: Hurricane Quillon Category 2 landfall triggered state of emergency in 10 Panhandle counties. FDEM has $46.75M direct operational cash for rapid Category A/B work (debris removal, emergency protective measures) before any federal major disaster declaration. Federal PA reimbursement (75%) takes months; counties must front costs. Five counties lack fiscal capacity to meet local share or front contracts (D7). Allocation prioritizes life safety (hospital generators) and counties unable to self-fund, while preserving 10% state reserve for contingencies.
assumptions: No federal major disaster declaration approved as of 2026-10-11 (D9).
Category A/B work eligible for 75% federal / 17.5% state / 7.5% local cost share (D4).
FDEM cash advance pool of $46.75M covers state+local share advances for Category A/B (D3, D5).
Counties with >30 days cash on hand can front initial costs (D7).
Hospital generator fuel is Category B emergency protective measure funded within county allocation.
Pre-event debris contracts EX-DR-01/02/03 mobilizing 2026-10-12 (D8).

assessments.analyst: Challenging the Negotiator's proposal (version 2) on three material grounds that remain unresolved from round 1: (1) Hospital generator fuel costs for 6 hospitals (Bay 2, Escambia 1, Gulf 1, Franklin 1, Calhoun 1) are embedded in county allocations but FEMA PA Category B eligibility for generator fuel costs remains unconfirmed; D8 shows 310,000 gallons under contract but pricing unknown, and FEMA PA policy guides (S11, S25, S26) do not explicitly confirm generator fuel reimbursement eligibility under Category B emergency protective measures. (2) Franklin County's $320K payroll gap embedded in its $1.87M allocation assumes FEMA PA payroll reimbursement eligibility, but S15 confirms FEMA only reimburses labor costs consistent with pre-disaster written policies; Franklin's payroll documentation policies not verified as FEMA-compliant (evidence request E2 declined), creating reimbursement risk for the $320K advance. (3) The 12.2% proportional reduction for five fiscally stronger counties (Bay, Escambia, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Walton) uses preliminary D5 allocation ratios that D9 states are preliminary and may alter after joint damage assessments beginning 2026-10-13; the 12.2% reduction lacks a documented methodology tied to quantified fiscal capacity metrics (days cash on hand: 45, 60, 55, 40, 50; reserve adequacy ratios vary 3.5x-7.6x local share). Also flagging unresolved reserve adequacy: 10% state reserve ($4.675M) untested against multi-month federal reimbursement timeline while five counties have <3 weeks cash (Franklin 7 days, Gulf 9, Calhoun 5, Wakulla 18, Washington 12). Requesting evidence on FEMA PA generator fuel eligibility and federal declaration timeline.
assessments.risk: Challenging the round 1 proposal (version 2) on three critical risk grounds that remain unresolved: (1) The 10% state reserve ($4.675M) is untested against the multi-month federal reimbursement timeline; D9 confirms no federal major disaster declaration submitted yet and D7/D9 indicate reimbursement typically months after obligation, while five fiscally distressed counties have <3 weeks cash on hand (Franklin 7 days, Gulf 9, Calhoun 5, Wakulla 18, Washington 12). The reserve may be exhausted before any federal reimbursement arrives, leaving no funds for continued advances to counties that cannot front costs. (2) Franklin County's $320K payroll bridge embedded in its $1.87M allocation assumes FEMA PA payroll reimbursement eligibility, but S15 (FEMA PAPPG v5) explicitly requires pre-disaster written labor policies that withstand scrutiny: 'FEMA only reimburses labor costs that are consistent with the Applicant's written policy that is in place and used prior to the incident' and 'This is not something you want to figure out after the disaster.' Franklin's payroll documentation policies have not been verified as FEMA-compliant (evidence request E2 declined), creating material reimbursement risk for the advance. (3) Hospital generator fuel costs for six hospitals (Bay 2, Escambia 1, Gulf 1, Franklin 1, Calhoun 1) are embedded in five county allocations but FEMA Category B eligibility for generator fuel costs remains unconfirmed; D8 shows 310,000 gallons under contract with pricing unknown, and FEMA PA policy guides (S11, S18, S19, S42) describe Category B emergency protective measures but do not explicitly confirm generator fuel reimbursement eligibility. This creates reimbursement risk for fuel costs embedded in county allocations. Additionally flagging the Analyst's O15:
assessments.strategy: Challenge the round 1 proposal (version 2) on three strategic grounds: (1) Single-phase commitment of $42.075M (90% of cash pool) before any federal major disaster declaration is submitted creates unrecoverable exposure if declaration is delayed or denied; D9 confirms request not yet submitted and joint assessments begin 2026-10-13, while S29/S30 show even for Hurricane Milton (Cat 4) the major declaration took 2 days and 100% federal share was limited to 90 days. (2) The 12.2% uniform reduction across five fiscally stronger counties ignores their tiered cash-on-hand (Bay 45d, Escambia 60d, Okaloosa 55d, Santa Rosa 40d, Walton 50d per D7); a tiered reduction keyed to days-of-cash would preserve more advance capacity for counties that cannot front costs while still fitting within the $42.075M allocation ceiling. (3) Hospital generator fuel costs for six hospitals (Bay 2, Escambia 1, Gulf 1, Franklin 1, Calhoun 1) and Franklin's $320K payroll bridge are embedded in allocations but FEMA Category B eligibility for generator fuel is not confirmed in PAPPG v5 (S11, S12, S26 describe eligible EPMs but do not list generator fuel; S50 addresses generators under HMGP/PDM not PA Category B; S48 mentions generator equipment for COVID-19 Category B but not fuel), and FEMA payroll reimbursement requires pre-disaster written policies (S15) which Franklin has not verified. These create material reimbursement risk for advances to counties that cannot front costs.

Three material objections from round 1 remain unresolved: (1) Generator fuel eligibility under Category B unconfirmed in PAPPG v5; (2) Franklin County payroll bridge assumes FEMA PA payroll reimbursement but S15 requires pre-disaster written policies; (3) 12.2% uniform reduction lacks methodology tied to fiscal capacity metrics. Need to verify PAPPG v5 Category B eligible work list for generator fuel and federal reimbursement timeline for Florida major disasters.

findings.claim: No federal major disaster declaration submitted; joint assessments begin 2026-10-13; no federal funds obligated until declaration approved
findings.explanation: Challenge the round 1 proposal (version 2) on three strategic grounds: (1) Single-phase commitment of $42.075M (90% of cash pool) before any federal major disaster declaration is submitted creates unrecoverable exposure if declaration is delayed or denied; D9 confirms request not yet submitted and joint assessments begin 2026-10-13, while S29/S30 show even for Hurricane Milton (Cat 4) the major declaration took 2 days and 100% federal share was limited to 90 days. (2) The 12.2% uniform reduction across five fiscally stronger counties ignores their tiered cash-on-hand (Bay 45d, Escambia 60d, Okaloosa 55d, Santa Rosa 40d, Walton 50d per D7); a tiered reduction keyed to days-of-cash would preserve more advance capacity for counties that cannot front costs while still fitting within the $42.075M allocation ceiling. (3) Hospital generator fuel costs for six hospitals (Bay 2, Escambia 1, Gulf 1, Franklin 1, Calhoun 1) and Franklin's $320K payroll bridge are embedded in allocations but FEMA Category B eligibility for generator fuel is not confirmed in PAPPG v5 (S11, S12, S26 describe eligible EPMs but do not list generator fuel; S50 addresses generators under HMGP/PDM not PA Category B; S48 mentions generator equipment for COVID-19 Category B but not fuel), and FEMA payroll reimbursement requires pre-disaster written policies (S15) which Franklin has not verified. These create material reimbursement risk for advances to counties that cannot front costs.

scenario.narrative: Hurricane Quillon Category 2 landfall triggered state of emergency in 10 Panhandle counties. FDEM has $46.75M direct operational cash for rapid Category A/B work before any federal major disaster declaration. Federal PA reimbursement (75%) takes months; counties must front costs. Five counties lack fiscal capacity to meet local share or front contracts (D7). Two-phase advance structure limits exposure: Phase 1 immediate for 5 fiscally distressed counties (<3 weeks cash); Phase 2 contingent for 5 stronger counties released only after federal declaration submission. Tiered reductions keyed to days-of-cash-on-hand (D7) preserve capacity for distressed counties. Franklin payroll bridge conditional on FEMA-compliant policies (S15). Hospital generator fuel qualifies as Category B life-safety measures (S11, S25).
assumptions: No federal major disaster declaration submitted as of 2026-10-11 (D9); joint assessments begin 2026-10-13.
Category A/B work eligible for 75% federal / 17.5% state / 7.5% local cost share (D4).
FDEM cash advance pool of $46.75M covers state+local share advances for Category A/B (D3, D5).
Counties with >30 days cash on hand can front initial costs (D7).
Hospital generator fuel is Category B emergency protective measure for life-safety (eliminate immediate threats to lives/public health) per S11, S25.
Pre-event debris contracts EX-DR-01/02/03 mobilizing 2026-10-12 (D8).
Franklin County payroll documentation not verified as FEMA-compliant (S15, E2 declined); payroll bridge conditional.
Fuel contract pricing unknown (D8); documentation requirements flagged for each county.

assessments.negotiator: Researching official PAPPG v5 Chapter 7 text for explicit Category B eligible work list including generator fuel costs, and federal reimbursement timeline for Florida major disaster declarations 2024-2025.
assessments.analyst: Challenge the Negotiator's proposal (version 2) on three material grounds where resolutions do not close evidentiary gaps: (1) Hospital generator fuel for 6 hospitals embedded as Category B life-safety measures per S11/S25 general criteria, but PAPPG v5 (S44) does not explicitly confirm generator fuel cost eligibility under Category B emergency protective measures; S44 Chapter 7 lists generators under permanent work (Category F utilities), not Category B. Baker Donelson (S17) warns FEMA applies narrow interpretations and bright-line distinctions. (2) Franklin County $320K payroll bridge made conditional advance pending FEMA-compliant payroll policy verification (S15), but conditional status does not eliminate reimbursement risk — if policies are non-compliant, advance may be unrecoverable; evidence request E2 declined. (3) Tiered reductions keyed to days-of-cash-on-hand (D7) improve on uniform 12.2% but still use preliminary D5 allocation ratios that D9 states may alter after joint damage assessments beginning 2026-10-13; methodology documented but base ratios unstable. Additionally flag unresolved reserve adequacy: 10% state reserve ($4.675M) untested against multi-month federal reimbursement timeline while five counties have <3 weeks cash (Franklin 7d, Gulf 9d, Calhoun 5d, Wakulla 18d, Washington 12d). Evidence requests E1, E2, E12, E13 all declined by reviewer.
assessments.risk: Challenge the round 2 proposal (version 3) on three critical risk grounds where resolutions in the revision do not materially mitigate the underlying reimbursement and liquidity risks: (1) The $4.988M state reserve exceeds the $4.675M minimum by only $313K (0.67% of pool), yet five Phase 1 counties have 5-18 days cash on hand and federal PA reimbursement takes 'months after obligation' (D7). If federal declaration is delayed beyond 2-3 weeks, Phase 1 counties will need additional advances before any federal reimbursement arrives, exhausting the razor-thin reserve buffer. (2) Franklin County's $320K payroll bridge reclassified as 'conditional advance pending FEMA-compliant payroll policy verification' (S15) does not mitigate reimbursement risk — it merely defers it. Franklin has 7 days cash and payroll at risk within 2 weeks (D7); if its pre-disaster labor policies fail FEMA scrutiny (E2 declined), the $320K advance becomes unrecoverable, consuming 6.4% of the total reserve. (3) Hospital generator fuel for 6 hospitals embedded in five county allocations as Category B life-safety measures lacks confirmed FEMA PA Category B eligibility. S44 (PAPPG v5) Chapter 7 eligibility criteria do not explicitly list generator fuel costs; S59/S40 (secondary sources) mention 'fuel for emergency pumps' as eligible but the official PAPPG v5 does not confirm this in the extracted Chapter 7. Documentation requirements flagged in the proposal do not establish eligibility — they only document an unconfirmed cost category. These three risks remain materially unresolved despite the revision's reclassifications and flags.

No federal declaration submitted (D9). If declaration is delayed beyond 2-3 weeks, Phase 1 counties will need additional advances before any federal reimbursement arrives, exhausting the razor-thin reserve buffer. S44 (PAPPG v5) Chapter 7 eligibility criteria do not explicitly list generator fuel costs; S59/S40 mention 'fuel for emergency pumps' as eligible but the official PAPPG v5 extracted text does not confirm this in Chapter 7. (3) Franklin County's $320K payroll bridge reclassified as 'conditional advance pending FEMA-compliant payroll policy verification' (S15) does not mitigate reimbursement risk — it merely defers it. (1) Generator fuel cost eligibility under Category B Emergency Protective Measures remains unconfirmed in official PAPPG v5 Chapter 7 text - S55 secondary source mentions 'fuel for emergency pumps' as eligible but official extracted text (S44) is truncated before the explicit eligible work list. Six hospitals across five counties have fuel costs embedded in allocations totaling ~$5.3M+ Phase 1 + Phase 2 amounts. findings.explanation: Challenge the round 2 proposal (version 3) on three strategic grounds: (1) The $4.988M state reserve exceeds the $4.675M minimum by only $313K (0.67% of pool), yet five Phase 1 counties have 5-18 days cash on hand (D7) and federal PA reimbursement takes 'months after obligation' (D7). No federal declaration submitted (D9). If declaration is delayed beyond 2-3 weeks, Phase 1 counties will need additional advances before any federal reimbursement arrives, exhausting the razor-thin reserve buffer. (2) Hospital generator fuel for 6 hospitals embedded in five county allocations as Category B life-safety measures lacks confirmed FEMA PA Category B eligibility. S44 (PAPPG v5) Chapter 7 eligibility criteria do not explicitly list generator fuel costs; S59/S40 mention 'fuel for emergency pumps' as eligible but the official PAPPG v5 extracted text does not confirm this in Chapter 7. Documentation requirements flagged in the proposal do not establish eligibility — they only document an unconfirmed cost category. (3) Franklin County's $320K payroll bridge reclassified as 'conditional advance pending FEMA-compliant payroll policy verification' (S15) does not mitigate reimbursement risk — it merely defers it. Franklin has 7 days cash and payroll at risk within 2 weeks (D7); if its pre-disaster labor policies fail FEMA scrutiny per S15, the $320K advance becomes unrecoverable, consuming 6.4% of the total reserve. The conditional label does not reduce exposure for a county that cannot front costs.
findings.validation_note: Exact passage located; relevance still requires human review.

scenario.narrative: Hurricane Quillon Category 2 landfall triggered state of emergency in 10 Panhandle counties. FDEM has $46.75M direct operational cash for rapid Category A/B work before any federal major disaster declaration. Federal PA reimbursement (75%) takes months; counties must front costs. Five counties lack fiscal capacity to meet local share or front contracts (D7). Two-phase advance structure limits exposure: Phase 1 immediate for 5 fiscally distressed counties (<3 weeks cash); Phase 2 contingent for 5 stronger counties released only after federal declaration submission. Tiered reductions keyed to days-of-cash-on-hand (D7) preserve capacity for distressed counties. Franklin payroll bridge conditional on FEMA-compliant policies (S15). Hospital generator fuel qualifies as Category B life-safety measures (S11, S25).
assumptions: No federal major disaster declaration submitted as of 2026-10-11 (D9); joint assessments begin 2026-10-13.
Category A/B work eligible for 75% federal / 17.5% state / 7.5% local cost share (D4).
FDEM cash advance pool of $46.75M covers state+local share advances for Category A/B (D3, D5).
Counties with >30 days cash on hand can front initial costs (D7).
Hospital generator fuel is Category B emergency protective measure for life-safety (eliminate immediate threats to lives/public health) per S11, S25.
Pre-event debris contracts EX-DR-01/02/03 mobilizing 2026-10-12 (D8).
Franklin County payroll documentation not verified as FEMA-compliant (S15, E2 declined); payroll bridge conditional.
Fuel contract pricing unknown (D8); documentation requirements flagged for each county.

Challenge the round 1 proposal (version 2) on three strategic grounds: (1) Single-phase commitment of $42.075M (90% of cash pool) before any federal major disaster declaration is submitted creates unrecoverable exposure if declaration is delayed or denied; D9 confirms request not yet submitted and joint assessments begin 2026-10-13, while S29/S30 show even for Hurricane Milton (Cat 4) the major declaration took 2 days and 100% federal share was limited to 90 days. (2) The 12.2% uniform reduction across five fiscally stronger counties ignores their tiered cash-on-hand (Bay 45d, Escambia 60d, Okaloosa 55d, Santa Rosa 40d, Walton 50d per D7); a tiered reduction keyed to days-of-cash would preserve more advance capacity for counties that cannot front costs while still fitting within the $42.075M allocation ceiling. (3) Hospital generator fuel costs for six hospitals (Bay 2, Escambia 1, Gulf 1, Franklin 1, Calhoun 1) and Franklin's $320K payroll bridge are embedded in allocations but FEMA Category B eligibility for generator fuel is not confirmed in PAPPG v5 (S11, S12, S26 describe eligible EPMs but do not list generator fuel; S50 addresses generators under HMGP/PDM not PA Category B; S48 mentions generator equipment for COVID-19 Category B but not fuel), and FEMA payroll reimbursement requires pre-disaster written policies (S15) which Franklin has not verified. These create material reimbursement risk for advances to counties that cannot front costs.

messages.summary: As Stability, I assess the Negotiator's proposal for longer-term fiscal sustainability, implementation dependencies on federal declaration and reimbursement rules, and equitable distribution of benefits and burdens across counties with vastly different fiscal capacities. Three material objections arise: (1) Generator fuel eligibility under Category B is unconfirmed in current FEMA PAPPG v5; the proposal embeds fuel costs in five county allocations but S30 indicates FEMA takes a narrow view of eligible Emergency Protective Measures, creating reimbursement risk for allocated funds. (3) The 12.2% uniform reduction across five fiscally stronger counties lacks a documented, defensible methodology tied to quantified fiscal capacity metrics (days of cash on hand: 45, 60, 55, 40, 50; reserve adequacy ratios vary widely), creating arbitrary and potentially inequitable burden distribution. The single-phase commitment of 90% of the cash pool before the federal declaration timeline is known (D9: joint assessments begin 2026-10-13) creates implementation dependency risk if reimbursement rules exclude embedded costs.

messages.summary: Vote: conditional_support. The two-phase structure with tiered reductions keyed to days-of-cash-on-hand (D7) materially improves on the uniform 12.2% reduction and limits initial exposure to $8.095M for the five fiscally distressed counties (<3 weeks cash). Franklin payroll bridge correctly reclassified as conditional advance pending FEMA-compliant policy verification (S15). (2) Franklin $320K conditional advance does not eliminate reimbursement risk — if pre-disaster labor policies non-compliant, advance unrecoverable; Franklin has 7 days cash, payroll at risk within 2 weeks (D7). (3) Reserve adequacy fundamentally untested: $4.988M exceeds $4.675M minimum by only $313K (0.67%) while five Phase 1 counties have 5-18 days cash (D7) and federal PA reimbursement takes 'months after obligation' (D7) with no federal declaration submitted (D9). If declaration delayed beyond 2-3 weeks, Phase 1 counties will need additional advances before federal funds arrive, exhausting the razor-thin reserve. Tiered reductions (O27) still use preliminary D5 allocation ratios that D9 states may alter after joint assessments beginning 2026-10-13. Conditions: (a) Generator fuel eligibility must be verified via official PAPPG v5 Chapter 7 before costs incurred; (b) Franklin payroll policies must be verified FEMA-compliant before conditional advance released; (c) Reserve adequacy reassessed if federal declaration not submitted within 2 weeks; (d) Phase 2 allocations adjustable per final damage assessments.

messages.summary: Vote: oppose. The final proposal (version 4) fails to materially mitigate three critical reimbursement and liquidity risks that remain unresolved despite the revision's reclassifications and documentation flags. (1) Reserve adequacy: $4.988M reserve exceeds $4.675M minimum by only $313K (0.67% of pool) while five Phase 1 counties have 5-18 days cash on hand (D7) and federal PA reimbursement takes 'months after obligation' (D7) with no federal declaration submitted (D9). The two-phase structure limits initial exposure but does not close the fundamental liquidity gap — if declaration is delayed beyond 2-3 weeks, Phase 1 counties will need additional advances before any federal reimbursement arrives, exhausting the razor-thin reserve buffer. (2) Franklin payroll conditional advance: $320K reclassified as 'conditional advance pending FEMA-compliant payroll policy verification' (S15) merely defers reimbursement risk; it does not eliminate it. Franklin has 7 days cash, payroll at risk within 2 weeks (D7), evidence request E2 declined. If pre-disaster labor policies fail FEMA scrutiny per S15, the $320K advance becomes unrecoverable, consuming 6.4% of the total reserve. (3) Generator fuel Category B eligibility: Hospital generator fuel for 6 hospitals embedded in five county allocations as Category B life-safety measures lacks confirmed FEMA PA Category B eligibility in official PAPPG v5 Chapter 7 (S44 truncated; S55 secondary source only claims 'fuel for emergency pumps' eligible). Documentation requirements flagged in the proposal do not establish eligibility — they only document an unconfirmed cost category. These three risks remain materially unresolved. Objections O16, O17, O18 (and their round 3 counterparts O28-O36) were rejected in review (M13) and carried as deferred;

proposals.recommendation: Allocate $42,075,000 to counties for Category A/B emergency work (Debris Removal and Emergency Protective Measures), holding $4,675,000 state reserve. Gulf ($2,805,000), Franklin ($1,870,000), Calhoun ($935,000), Wakulla ($1,402,500), and Washington ($1,402,500) receive full eligibility as they cannot front costs. Bay ($10,263,000), Escambia ($8,209,000), Okaloosa ($6,157,000), Santa Rosa ($4,926,000), and Walton ($4,105,000) receive proportional reductions (12.2%) reflecting their ability to front costs for 30-60 days. Each county's allocation must cover hospital generator fuel where applicable (Bay, Escambia, Gulf, Franklin, Calhoun).

scenario.narrative: Hurricane Quillon Category 2 landfall triggered state of emergency in 10 Panhandle counties. FDEM has $46.75M direct operational cash for rapid Category A/B work (debris removal, emergency protective measures) before any federal major disaster declaration. Federal PA reimbursement (75%) takes months; counties must front costs. Five counties lack fiscal capacity to meet local share or front contracts (D7). Allocation prioritizes life safety (hospital generators) and counties unable to self-fund, while preserving 10% state reserve for contingencies.

The two-phase structure with tiered reductions keyed to days-of-cash-on-hand (D7) materially improves on the uniform 12.2% reduction and limits initial exposure to $8.095M for the five fiscally distressed counties (<3 weeks cash). (2) Franklin $320K conditional advance does not eliminate reimbursement risk — if pre-disaster labor policies non-compliant, advance unrecoverable; Franklin has 7 days cash, payroll at risk within 2 weeks (D7). If declaration delayed beyond 2-3 weeks, Phase 1 counties will need additional advances before federal funds arrive, exhausting the razor-thin reserve. Conditions: (a) Generator fuel eligibility must be verified via official PAPPG v5 Chapter 7 before costs incurred; (b) Franklin payroll policies must be verified FEMA-compliant before conditional advance released; (c) Reserve adequacy reassessed if federal declaration not submitted within 2 weeks; (d) Phase 2 allocations adjustable per final damage assessments.

results.title: FEMA Approves Nearly $97 Million to Support Recovery in Florida | FEMA.gov
results.content:
Release Date:

April 24, 2026

LAKE MARY, Fla. — FEMA announced nearly $97 million in funding to support recovery for past disasters in Florida for Public Assistance projects. Through Public Assistance, FEMA empowers state and local communities to recover following a major disaster, including debris removal, emergency protective measures and the repair or replacement of public infrastructure damaged by recent disasters. [...] More than $19 million to reimburse costs for power restoration and distribution systems, including $11.2 million for Lee County Electric Cooperative for Hurricane Ian, $4 million for Sumter Electric Cooperative following Hurricane Milton and $1.1 million for Central Florida Electric Cooperative for Hurricane Helene.
 More than $17.3 million for countywide debris removal following Hurricane Ian in Sarasota County.
 Nearly $12.3 million for the City of Tallahassee’s debris removal and emergency response following severe storms in 2024. [...] FEMA is reimbursing these costs at no less than 75% federal share. Since January 2025, more than $2 billion has been provided to Florida to support the state’s infrastructure repair and rebuilding. We will continue to work closely with Florida to support communities through the state-led recovery efforts.

###

FEMA’s mission is helping people before, during and after disasters.

| |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | | |  | | --- | | Within the Public Assistance Program, there are two general types of work: Emergency Work and Permanent Work. To facilitate the processing of Public Assistance grant funding, FEMA separates Emergency Work into two categories, based on the type of work performed. Permanent Work is separated into five categories based on facility types. | | [Select this link for a full image description.](javascript: if ( typeof(NewGrouping) != 'undefined' ) {NewGrouping('86772052415324B1DAED130B003791E2','1');}) | | |

Emergency Work

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  | | --- | --- | | |  | | --- | | Public Assistance Emergency Work is work which must be done immediately to:   * Save lives * Protect public health and safety * Protect improved property * Eliminate or lessen an immediate threat of additional damage   Emergency Work is made up of two Categories of Work:   * Category A - Debris Removal * Category B - Emergency Protective Measures   An Applicant has six months from the declaration or designation date to complete their eligible Emergency Work, unless the Recipient or FEMA authorizes an extension. | | |

Emergency Protective Measures

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  | | --- | --- | | |  | | --- | | This course focuses on Category B, Emergency Protective Measures, of Emergency Work under the Public Assistance program.  Emergency Protective Measures are temporary measures taken against an incident. As outlined in the Public Assistance Program and Policy Guide, 2.VI.B,  Emergency Protective Measures are actions taken before, during, and after an incident to save lives, protect public health and safety, and prevent damage to improved public and private property. | | |

Emergency Protective Measures Eligibility

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  | | --- | --- | | |  | | --- | | Emergency Protective Measures conducted before, during, and after an incident are generally eligible if the measures:   * Eliminate or lessen immediate threats to lives, public health, or safety * Eliminate or lessen immediate threats of significant additional damage to improved public or private property in a cost-effective manner   Emergency Protective Measures eligibility is typically based on evaluation of the immediate threat and legal authority to perform the work.  FEMA may require validation by State, Local, Tribal, or Territorial government officials that a threat exists, including:   * Identification and evaluation of the threat * Recommendations of the work necessary to minimize the threat | | |

Emergency Protective Measures Cost-effectiveness

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| |  | | --- | | Another aspect of eligibility is cost-effectiveness. Certain projects must be cost-effective for Applicants to be eligible for grant funding from the Public Assistance program.   * Emergency Protective Measures that eliminate or lessen an immediate threat to lives, public health, and/or safety **do not** have to be cost-effective * Emergency Protective Measures that eliminate or lessen an immediate threat to protect improved property **must be** cost-effective | |

Linking Emergency Protective Measures to a Declared Event

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| |  | | --- | | As stated previously, Emergency Protective Measures conducted before, during, and after an incident are generally eligible.  Some activities that may qualify as Emergency Protective Measures include:   * Firefighting * Search and rescue * Evacuation and sheltering   Throughout response operations, it is important to track activities that are potentially eligible for reimbursement under the Public Assistance grant program. Without tracking Emergency Protective Measures, an Applicant may jeopardize Public Assistance grant funding. | |

Lesson 1 Summary

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| |  | | --- | | Emergency Protective Measures are temporary measures taken against an incident.  In this lesson, participants learned how to:   * Identify administrative requirements of the course * State the goals and objectives of the course * Define emergency protective measures   The next lesson provides an in-depth look at the activities that qualify as Emergency Protective Measures eligible under the Public Assistance Program. | |

Hurricane Milton Recovery: Brief Overview of FEMA Programs and Resources 

Updated October 13, 2024 (IN12438) 

Introduction

On October 9, 2024, Hurricane Milton made [landfall](https://apnews.com/article/hurricane-helene-florida-georgia-mexico-42fb7cc90604b7f87179920f97627873) as a [Category 4](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutsshws.php) hurricane in Florida's Tampa Bay area bringing heavy rain, storm surge, and floods to many counties on the coast and in the interior of the state. Some areas in the state are still actively recovering from [Hurricane Helene](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12429).

President Biden had previously issued an [emergency declaration](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/3622) for this storm on October 7, under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act(the Stafford Act, [P.L. 93-288](https://www.congress.gov/bill/93rd-congress/senate-bill/3062/text), as amended; [42 U.S.C. §§5121 et seq.](http://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?path=/prelim@title42/chapter68&edition=prelim)), authorizing [Public Assistance (PA)](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF11529) for [emergency protective measures](https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_pappg-v4-updated-links_policy_6-1-2020.pdf#page=111)put into action beginning October 5, 2024. On October 8,2024, President Biden issued another [emergency declaration](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/3623) authorizing federal assistance to Seminole Tribe of Florida.

As of October 11, President Biden declared a [major disaster for Hurricane Milton](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/4834) in Florida, [authorizing PA, Individual Assistance](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF11298), and [Hazard Mitigation Assistance](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN11187). President Biden also [increased the federal share of eligible response costs](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/10/12/president-joseph-r-biden-jr-approves-florida-disaster-declaration-8/); the federal government will cover 100% of eligible costs of PA provided for emergency protective measures and debris removal for a period of 90 days.

The situation remains dynamic; additional declarations, or additional forms of assistance are expected given Milton's impact.

Information about state and county disaster assistance is published in FEMA's [declaration database](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/declarations). [FEMA's Hurricane Milton web p a ge](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/current/hurricane-milton) provides information on how to apply for disaster assistance. FEMA has also created [another site to dispel rumors and misinformation](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/current/hurricane-helene/rumor-response) related to aid to survivors, evacuation, and relief funding.

FEMA Emergency and Major Disaster Assistance

FEMA provides three major categories of disaster assistance, some of which may be available pursuant to an emergency declaration and/or a major disaster declaration:

*   [_Public Assistance_](https://www.fema.gov/assistance/public)(PA) provides grants and direct assistance to state, tribal, territorial, and local governments, and certain private nonprofit organizations, for emergency work (e.g., debris removal and [emergency protective measures](https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_pappg-v4-updated-links_policy_6-1-2020.pdf#page=111)), and permanent work (for rebuilding and replacement of disaster-damaged facilities). 
*   [_Individual Assistance_](https://www.fema.gov/assistance/individual)(IA) supports disaster survivors, including through grants of financial assistance and direct assistance to affected individuals and households for housing and financial assistance for other needs, and crisis counseling (both may be authorized pursuant to either an emergency or major disaster declaration), as well as case management services, legal services, and disaster unemployment assistance (may only be authorized pursuant to a major disaster declaration). 
*   [_Hazard Mitigation Grant Program_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN11187)(HMGP) funds mitigation and resiliency projects and programs, typically across the entire state or territory (can only be authorized pursuant to a major disaster declaration). 

The forms of assistance authorized by a declaration may vary by the [designated areas](https://www.ecfr.gov/cgi-bin/text-idx?SID=c41c4e25e985d2afea0c6e109f166e93&mc=true&node=se44.1.206_140&rgn=div8), per the declaration (subject to amendment). The President can also amend emergency and major disaster declarations to decrease the [cost-share requirements](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47646) for [PA](https://www.ecfr.gov/cgi-bin/text-idx?SID=4bf28e2644255919b530fcd3957de6bf&mc=true&node=se44.1.206_147&rgn=div8).

National Flood Insurance Program

The [National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN10450) is the primary source of flood insurance coverage for residential properties. Homeowners and tenants with NFIP flood insurance can make flood damage claims using the normal [NFIP claims process.](https://www.floodsmart.gov/how-do-i-start-my-flood-claim) There does not have to be an emergency or disaster declaration in order to make an NFIP claim. Policyholders can make a claim as soon as they can safely return to their property to document the damage.

As of September 30, 2024, the NFIP had $5.001 billion available to pay claims. If claims from Hurricane Milton are more than this, FEMA could [borrow up to $9.9 billion](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN10784) from the Treasury. FEMA could also potentially receive up to [$619.5 million](https://www.fema.gov/press-release/20240103/fema-announces-reinsurance-program-manage-future-flood-risk-2024) of [reinsurance](https://www.fema.gov/flood-insurance/work-with-nfip/reinsurance)if losses from Hurricane Milton are between $7 billion and $11 billion. The NFIP is currently authorized until [December 20, 2024](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/9747/text).

Federal Funding for Disaster Response and Recovery

While it is not the only source of federal funding for disaster assistance, FEMA's [Disaster Relief Fund](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R43537) (DRF) is the primary funding source for federal government response and recovery activities. As a result, its level of unobligated funds is often used as a proxy for the overall availability of federal resources for response and recovery.

On August 7, 2024,[prior to the development of Hurricane Helene, FEMA announced the implementation of immediate needs funding (INF) restrictions](https://content.govdelivery.com/attachments/USDHSFEMA/2023/08/29/file_attachments/2597953/FEMA%20Advisory%20FEMA%20Announces%20Implementation%20of%20Immediate%20Needs%20Funding%2020230829.pdf), as a result of the unobligated balance in the DRF for major disasters being [at risk of depletion before the end of FY2024](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47676). [INF slows obligations for long-term recovery and mitigation projects](https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_ocfo-inf-fact-sheet.pdf) in favor of preserving resources for response and recovery activities. Although annual appropriations have not been enacted for FEMA as of the date on this Insight, on September 26, 2024, President Biden signed into law a [continuing resolution](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48189)([P.L. 118-83](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/9747/text)) that provides $20.26 billion in temporary budget authority for the DRF, which became available October 1. When those funds became available, FEMA lifted INF restrictions and resumed obligating funds for more than $8 billion of long-term recovery and mitigation projects that had been delayed.

These funds will be available for Stafford Act disaster assistance programs until December 20, 2024, or until FEMA's annual appropriations are enacted, whichever comes first. If the CR expires, that temporary budget authority will no longer be available, and FEMA's disaster response and recovery functions will be severely constrained.

CRS Resources

**Hurricane and Flooding Resources**

*   CRS Report R46408, [_Hurricane Events: CRS Experts_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46408)
*   CRS Report R40882, [_Flooding Events: CRS Experts_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R40882)
*   CRS Report R44593, [_Introduction to the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R44593)
*   CRS Report R45017, [_Flood Resilience and Risk Reduction: Federal Assistance and Programs_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R45017)

**Federal Disaster Assistance—Process and Programs**

*   CRS Report WMR10001, _CRS Guide to Federal Emergency Management_
*   CRS Report RL31734, [_Federal Disaster Assistance Response and Recovery Programs: Brief Summaries_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RL31734)
*   CRS Report R41981, [_Congressional Primer on Responding to and Recovering from Major Disasters and Emergencies_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R41981)
*   CRS Report R47676, [_Disaster Relief Fund State of Play: In Brief_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47676)
*   CRS Report R46749, [_FEMA's Public Assistance Program: A Primer and Considerations for Congress_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46749)
*   CRS Report R46014, [_FEMA Individual Assistance Programs: An Overview_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46014)
*   CRS Insight IN11187, [_Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Hazard Mitigation Assistance_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN11187)
*   CRS Report R47631, [_Federal Disaster Assistance for Businesses: Summaries and Policy Options_](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47631)
